subject: chemistry
title: Half equations at the electrodes
key_idea: (AQA: Higher tier) A half equation shows what happens to one ion at one electrode. At the cathode, positive ions gain electrons, which is reduction. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons, which is oxidation. Both the atoms and the charges must balance.

sections.heading: Reduction and oxidation at the electrodes

blocks.text: (AQA: Higher tier) This section covers what happens to ions at each electrode.

items.meaning: An equation for the reaction of one ion at one electrode, showing the electrons gained or lost.
A reaction in which electrons are gained.
A reaction in which electrons are lost.

items: At the **cathode** (negative electrode), positive ions gain electrons. The reaction is **reduction**.
At the **anode** (positive electrode), negative ions lose electrons. The reaction is **oxidation**.
So reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation happens at the anode.
Cathode: ions gain electrons, so reduction.
Anode: ions lose electrons, so oxidation.

blocks.text: (AQA: Higher tier) This section covers how to write and balance a half equation.

blocks.label: A half equation at the cathode (reduction)
where: Cu²⁺ is the copper ion, with a 2+ charge
e⁻ is an electron, on the left because it is gained

blocks.label: A half equation at the anode (oxidation)
where: Cl⁻ is the chloride ion, with a 1− charge
e⁻ is an electron, on the right because it is lost

blocks.text: The electrons go on the left for a gain and on the right for a loss. A loss can also be written as a subtraction on the left, for example 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ → Cl₂.

items.text: Two oxide ions are needed to make one O₂ molecule: 2O²⁻ → O₂.
The left side has a charge of 4−. The right side has no charge. Add 4 electrons on the right.

blocks.text: The Zn²⁺, Al³⁺ and O²⁻ equations apply to molten compounds. In aqueous solution, H⁺ ions are discharged instead of ions of metals more reactive than hydrogen.

diagram.alt: Sort half equations by the electrode where they happen.
diagram.prompt: Which electrode does each half equation happen at?

items: Metal ions and H⁺ gain electrons at the cathode, so the electrons are on the left.
Non-metal ions lose electrons at the anode, so the electrons are on the right.
Balance the atoms first, then balance the charge with electrons.

checks.q: Write the half equation for the reaction at the negative electrode when molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
Write the half equation for chloride ions forming chlorine at the positive electrode. State the type of reaction.
checks.a: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Oxidation, because the ions lose electrons.

checks.q: What type of reaction happens at the negative electrode, and why?
checks.a: Reduction, because the positive ions gain electrons.

worked_example.question:
Copper and chlorine are produced when molten copper chloride is electrolysed.

Complete the half equation for the reaction at each electrode.

Half equation at negative electrode: Cu²⁺ → ...
Half equation at positive electrode: 2Cl⁻ → ...
worked_example.tip: Multiples are allowed. 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ → Cl₂ is also accepted.

worked_example.question:
When molten zinc chloride is electrolysed, zinc ions, Zn²⁺, form zinc atoms.

Write the half equation for this reaction.
worked_example.tip: 1 mark for the correct species in the correct place and 1 mark for balancing. State symbols are ignored.

worked_example.question:
Chromium is used for electroplating.

Chromium atoms lose electrons at the anode.

Chromium ions, Cr³⁺, gain electrons at the cathode.

Write balanced half equations to show the reactions at each electrode.

Anode ______
Cathode ______
answer_points: Anode: Cr → Cr³⁺ + 3e⁻ (1 mark for the formulae, 1 mark for balancing).
Cathode: Cr³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Cr (1 mark for the formulae, 1 mark for balancing).
worked_example.tip: Correct multiples are allowed. Cr − 3e⁻ → Cr³⁺ is also allowed.

worked_example.question:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate undergoes electrolysis using graphite electrodes.
Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
answer_points: O₂ is written as a product.
The equation is balanced for atoms and charge.
worked_example.tip: One mark for oxygen as a product, one for OH⁻ and electrons, one for the correct balanced equation.

worked_example.question:
When copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed, copper forms at the negative electrode.
Describe how copper metal forms at the negative electrode.
answer_points: Copper ions, Cu²⁺, are positively charged.
They are attracted to the negative electrode.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score. A correct half equation, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, earns the first and third points.
